meta.title: Development Law Docket
meta.what_this_is: Indian court judgments that changed what development organisations, state programmes and rights-holders can actually do.
meta.what_this_is_not: Legal advice. Holdings are summarised editorially; the linked judgment is authoritative. Case law changes — check the status field and the date.
meta.verification: Every entry's case name and decision year were checked against the judgment text, and each entry lists the specific terms confirmed present in that text. Summaries of what a case means are editorial and were not separately adjudicated.

judgments.case: Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa
judgments.holding: Found serious gaps in POSH implementation across public and private institutions and directed verification that Internal Committees actually exist and function.
judgments.what_changed: Put institutions on notice that a committee whose members and procedure cannot be evidenced is treated as no committee at all. Directly relevant to NGOs relying on a nominal ICC.
judgments.source_title: Aureliano Fernandes vs State Of Goa . on 12 May, 2023

judgments.case: Deepika Singh v. Central Administrative Tribunal
judgments.holding: Atypical families — including single-parent, queer and reconstituted households — are entitled to equal protection of benefits like maternity leave.
judgments.what_changed: Widens 'family' in benefit administration, relevant to HR policy and to programme eligibility criteria that assume a nuclear household.
judgments.source_title: Deepika Singh vs Central Administrative Tribunal on 16 August, 2022

judgments.case: Noel Harper v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Upheld the 2020 FCRA amendments, including the bar on transferring foreign contribution to other organisations and mandatory SBI New Delhi account opening.
judgments.what_changed: Ends the sub-granting model. An organisation receiving foreign funds cannot pass them to a partner, which reshapes how intermediary and consortium funding is structured in India.
judgments.source_title: Noel Harper vs Union Of India on 8 April, 2022

judgments.case: X v. Principal Secretary, Health & Family Welfare, NCT of Delhi
judgments.holding: Unmarried women are entitled to termination up to 24 weeks on the same terms as married women; 'husband' in the MTP Rules is read as 'partner'.
judgments.what_changed: Removed marital status as a gate on abortion access, and recognised marital rape for the limited purpose of the MTP Act.
judgments.source_title: X vs The Principal Secretary Health And ... on 29 September, 2022

judgments.case: State of Kerala v. Leesamma Joseph
judgments.holding: Reservation for persons with disabilities applies to promotion, not only to entry-level recruitment.
judgments.what_changed: Closed the loophole by which disabled employees were recruited under quota and then held at the same grade for a career.
judgments.source_title: The State Of Kerala vs Leesamma Joseph on 28 June, 2021

judgments.case: Vikash Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission
judgments.holding: Reasonable accommodation is a substantive right, not a concession; denying a scribe to a candidate with writer's cramp because he fell outside the benchmark-disability category was discriminatory.
judgments.what_changed: Broke the assumption that RPwD entitlements begin only at 40% benchmark disability. Accommodation is owed on the basis of need, which changes exam, workplace and service-delivery practice.
judgments.source_title: Vikash Kumar vs Union Public Service Commission on 11 February, 2021

judgments.case: Alembic Pharmaceuticals v. Rohit Prajapati
judgments.holding: Ex post facto environmental clearance is contrary to law; a project cannot regularise construction already carried out without clearance.
judgments.what_changed: Removes the 'build first, regularise later' route that had become routine, and is the citation for challenging retrospective clearances.
judgments.source_title: Alembic Pharmaceuticals Ltd. vs Rohit Prajapati . on 1 April, 2020

judgments.case: Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya
judgments.holding: Directed grant of permanent commission to women officers in the Army, rejecting arguments from physiological differences and troop attitudes.
judgments.what_changed: Named stereotype-based justification as discrimination — reasoning that transfers directly to any employer defending exclusion on grounds of 'suitability'.
judgments.source_title: Secr.,Ministry Of Defence vs Babita Puniya on 17 February, 2020

judgments.case: Indian Social Action Forum (INSAF) v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Read down the 'organisation of a political nature' provisions so that ordinary advocacy and rights work does not, by itself, disqualify an organisation from foreign funding.
judgments.what_changed: Protects issue-based campaigning from being classed as political activity — the distinction most likely to be argued in an FCRA proceeding against an NGO.
judgments.source_title: Indian Social Action Forum(Insaf) vs Union Of India on 6 March, 2020

judgments.case: In Re: Problems and Miseries of Migrant Labourers
judgments.holding: In suo motu proceedings during the COVID-19 lockdown, directed transport, dry rations and registration for stranded migrant workers.
judgments.what_changed: Produced the direction to build a national database of unorganised workers, and stands as the record of what the absence of one cost.
judgments.source_title: In Re Problems And Miseries Of Migrant ... vs In The Supreme Court Of India on 26 May, 2020

judgments.case: Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Suspended an airport's environmental clearance for non-disclosure and inadequate appraisal, holding that the EIA process must be substantively, not formally, complied with.
judgments.what_changed: Establishes that an incomplete or misleading EIA is a ground to set clearance aside — the practical basis for scrutinising project disclosures.
judgments.source_title: Hanuman Laxman Aroskar vs Union Of India on 29 March, 2019

judgments.case: CPIO, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal
judgments.holding: The office of the Chief Justice of India is a public authority under the RTI Act; judicial independence is not a blanket exemption from disclosure.
judgments.what_changed: Removed the argument that a constitutional office sits outside the RTI Act, while keeping a public-interest balancing test for personal information.
judgments.source_title: Cen.Pub.Information Officer,Sci . vs Subhash Chandra Agarwal on 13 November, 2019

judgments.case: Common Cause v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Recognised the right to die with dignity, permitting passive euthanasia and advance directives with procedural safeguards.
judgments.what_changed: Established the living will in India and made withdrawal of life support lawful under a defined procedure.
judgments.status_note: A Constitution Bench simplified the advance-directive procedure in 2023 after the original safeguards proved unworkable in practice. Follow the revised procedure, not the 2018 one.
judgments.source_title: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) vs Union Of India on 9 March, 2018

judgments.case: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Struck down adultery as a criminal offence, holding it treated a wife as her husband's property.
judgments.what_changed: Cited well beyond adultery, for the proposition that laws resting on a woman's subordinate status fail Article 14.
judgments.source_title: Joseph Shine vs Union Of India on 27 September, 2018

judgments.case: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Section 377 IPC is unconstitutional insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual acts between adults.
judgments.what_changed: Decriminalisation removed the threat that made outreach to LGBTQ+ communities legally hazardous, and reframed programme design around dignity rather than risk.
judgments.source_title: Navtej Singh Johar vs Union Of India Ministry Of Law And ... on 6 September, 2018

judgments.case: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar)
judgments.holding: Upheld Aadhaar for subsidies and welfare under Section 7, struck down mandatory linking by private entities and Section 57.
judgments.what_changed: Limits when Aadhaar may be demanded. A private organisation cannot require it, and exclusion caused by authentication failure remains a live ground of challenge.
judgments.source_title: Justice K.S.Puttaswamy(Retd) vs Union Of India on 26 September, 2018

judgments.case: Sampurna Behura v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Sampurna Behrua vs Union Of India on 9 February, 2018
judgments.holding: Found the Juvenile Justice Act substantially unimplemented and directed States to fill vacancies and constitute the bodies the Act requires.
judgments.what_changed: Makes the absence of Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards a matter of court-supervised compliance rather than an administrative backlog.

judgments.case: Disabled Rights Group v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Directed enforcement of the statutory reservation for persons with disabilities in higher education institutions, including centrally funded ones.
judgments.what_changed: Gave disability-rights organisations an enforceable handle on institutions that had treated the education quota as optional.
judgments.source_title: Disabled Right Group vs Union Of India on 15 December, 2017

judgments.case: Independent Thought v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Read down the exception permitting marital intercourse with a wife aged 15 to 18, making it rape.
judgments.what_changed: Removed the contradiction under which a girl was protected by POCSO and unprotected by the marital exception. Practically important for child-marriage casework.
judgments.source_title: Independent Thought vs Union Of India on 11 October, 2017

judgments.case: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Privacy)
judgments.holding: A nine-judge bench held privacy is a fundamental right intrinsic to Article 21, and set a proportionality test for any intrusion.
judgments.what_changed: Every data-collection decision in Indian development work now sits under a proportionality test: legality, necessity, proportionality, procedural safeguards. The foundation of the DPDP Act.
judgments.source_title: Justice K.S.Puttaswamy(Retd) And Anr. vs Union Of India And Ors. on 24 August, 2017

judgments.case: Rajive Raturi v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Directed Union and State governments to make public buildings, transport and information accessible within fixed timelines under the RPwD Act.
judgments.what_changed: Converted accessibility from an aspiration in the Act into a supervised programme with deadlines, and gave organisations a citation for demanding accessible premises and formats.
judgments.source_title: Rajive Raturi vs Union Of India on 15 December, 2017

judgments.case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Set aside instant triple talaq as arbitrary and not protected as an essential religious practice.
judgments.what_changed: Removed unilateral instant divorce, changing the legal position for Muslim women in maintenance and matrimonial casework.
judgments.status_note: Followed by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, which criminalised the pronouncement. The statute, and the debate over criminalisation, now govern practice.
judgments.source_title: Shayara Bano vs Union Of India And Ors. Ministry Of Women ... on 22 August, 2017

judgments.case: Devika Biswas v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Devika Biswas vs Union Of India . on 14 September, 2016
judgments.holding: Condemned mass sterilisation camps as a violation of reproductive autonomy and Article 21, and directed States to close camp-based targets.
judgments.what_changed: Ends the defence that a sterilisation camp is acceptable because it meets a family-planning target. Directly relevant to anyone working on reproductive health delivery.

judgments.case: Jeeja Ghosh v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Offloading a passenger with cerebral palsy without assessment violated her dignity; the Court awarded compensation and stressed the social model of disability.
judgments.what_changed: Made dignity, not medical fitness, the test for excluding a disabled person from a service — with damages attached, which is what gets service providers to change protocol.
judgments.source_title: Jeeja Ghosh vs Union Of India on 12 May, 2016

judgments.case: Swaraj Abhiyan v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Directed States to declare drought where conditions warranted and to implement NFSA and MGNREGA entitlements during it.
judgments.what_changed: Established that a State cannot avoid relief obligations by not declaring a drought — useful wherever a declaration is being withheld.
judgments.source_title: Swaraj Abhiyan vs Union Of India And Ors on 13 May, 2016

judgments.case: Laxmi v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Directed regulation of acid sales, compensation for survivors, and treatment obligations on hospitals.
judgments.what_changed: Created a concrete compensation and treatment entitlement, and made retail regulation a supervised obligation on States.
judgments.status_note: Relief was issued across several orders between 2013 and 2015 rather than in one judgment; cite the order relied on.
judgments.source_title: Laxmi vs Union Of India & Ors on 10 April, 2015

judgments.case: Reserve Bank of India v. Jayantilal N. Mistry
judgments.holding: A regulator cannot claim a fiduciary relationship with the entities it regulates to withhold inspection reports from the public.
judgments.what_changed: Strong authority against 'fiduciary capacity' refusals, which regulators and public bodies use routinely to deny disclosure about the institutions they oversee.
judgments.source_title: Reserve Bank Of India vs Jayantilal N. Mistry on 16 December, 2015

judgments.case: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as vague and overbroad, and read down intermediary takedown obligations.
judgments.what_changed: The governing authority on online speech, and on the limits of takedown demands against platforms.
judgments.status_note: Section 66A continues to be invoked by police years after being struck down — the Supreme Court has repeatedly had to reiterate that it is void. A charge under it is not merely wrong but a nullity.
judgments.source_title: Shreya Singhal vs U.O.I on 24 March, 2015

judgments.case: National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: National Legal Ser.Auth vs Union Of India & Ors on 15 April, 2014
judgments.holding: Recognised transgender persons as a third gender with the right to self-identify, and directed reservation and welfare measures.
judgments.what_changed: Gave transgender people a legal identity to assert against any registry, school or hospital that refused one — the ground every later gender-recognition claim in India stands on.
judgments.status_note: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 followed, and its self-identification procedure has been criticised as narrower than what NALSA required. Where the Act and the judgment differ, the constitutional standard in NALSA is the stronger argument.

judgments.case: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
judgments.holding: Registration of an FIR is mandatory where information discloses a cognizable offence; a preliminary inquiry is permitted only in limited categories.
judgments.what_changed: The citation used when a police station refuses to register a complaint — the single most common obstacle in frontline rights casework.
judgments.source_title: Lalita Kumari vs Govt.Of U.P.& Ors on 12 November, 2013

judgments.case: Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (Niyamgiri)
judgments.holding: Referred the question of religious and cultural rights over the Niyamgiri hills to the Gram Sabhas, whose decision would bind the clearance process.
judgments.what_changed: The strongest Indian authority for community consent over a project. Turned Forest Rights Act consultation into a decision the Gram Sabha actually makes.
judgments.source_title: Orissa Mining Corporation Ltd vs Ministry Of Environment & Forest &Ors on 18 April, 2013

judgments.case: Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. Central Information Commissioner
judgments.holding: Service records, assets and disciplinary details of a public servant are 'personal information' exempt under Section 8(1)(j) unless a larger public interest is shown.
judgments.what_changed: The single most-cited refusal ground in India. Any RTI request touching an individual official's record will meet it, so requests must be framed around a system or a decision rather than a person.
judgments.status_note: Still applied, and heavily criticised for being read far more broadly than its facts warrant. Later benches have narrowed its use where public interest is demonstrated, so cite the public-interest proviso in any appeal.
judgments.source_title: Girish Ramchandra Deshpande vs Cen.Information Commr.& Ors on 3 October, 2012

judgments.case: Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Found the Vishaka guidelines widely unimplemented and issued directions to States and regulators to bring complaints mechanisms into being.
judgments.what_changed: Established that non-implementation is itself actionable — a complainant can go to the High Court where an employer has simply not constituted a committee.
judgments.status_note: Directions were largely absorbed into the POSH Act, 2013 and its Rules. The case remains the authority on what happens when the machinery exists only on paper.
judgments.source_title: Medha Kotwal Lele & Ors vs U.O.I. & Ors on 19 October, 2012

judgments.case: Society for Un-aided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Society For Un-Aided P.School Of Raj vs U.O.I & Anr on 12 April, 2012
judgments.holding: Upheld the RTE Act's requirement that private unaided schools reserve 25% of Class I places for children from weaker and disadvantaged groups.
judgments.what_changed: Made the 25% quota enforceable against private schools, which is the provision most often resisted and the one most education-access work turns on.
judgments.status_note: A 2014 Constitution Bench held the 25% obligation does not apply to minority institutions, which narrows its reach considerably. Check the school's minority status before relying on it.

judgments.case: Bachpan Bachao Andolan v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Directed action against trafficking of children into circuses and for their rescue and rehabilitation.
judgments.what_changed: Established rescue-plus-rehabilitation as the standard: removing a child without a rehabilitation plan is not compliance.
judgments.source_title: Bachpan Bachao Andolan vs Union Of India & Ors on 18 April, 2011

judgments.case: Nandini Sundar v. State of Chhattisgarh
judgments.holding: Held the arming of civilians as Special Police Officers in counter-insurgency unconstitutional and directed disbanding of Salwa Judum.
judgments.what_changed: Central to conflict-affected programme work: the State cannot outsource force to irregulars, and the ruling names the harms that follow when it does.
judgments.source_title: Nandini Sundar & Ors vs State Of Chattisgarh on 5 July, 2011

judgments.case: Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration
judgments.holding: Reproductive choice is personal liberty under Article 21; pregnancy could not be terminated against the will of a woman with intellectual disability.
judgments.what_changed: Established that guardianship does not transfer reproductive decision-making, which is central to disability and institutional-care practice.
judgments.source_title: Suchita Srivastava & Anr vs Chandigarh Administration on 28 August, 2009

judgments.case: Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India
judgments.holding: Struck down a prohibition on women working in premises serving liquor as protective discrimination that failed strict scrutiny.
judgments.what_changed: The authority against 'for her own safety' restrictions on women's work — the State must fix the hazard, not exclude the worker.
judgments.source_title: Anuj Garg & Ors vs Hotel Association Of India & Ors on 6 December, 2007

judgments.case: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (ICDS / Anganwadi directions)
judgments.source_title: Peoples Union For Civil Liberties vs Union Of India And Ors on 9 July, 2007
judgments.holding: In the right-to-food litigation, directed that every sanctioned Anganwadi Centre be made operational and that ICDS reach children, adolescent girls, and pregnant and lactating women.
judgments.what_changed: Turned an ICDS sanction on paper into an operational obligation the State can be held to. This is the order to cite when a sanctioned centre exists in the records and not in the village.
judgments.status_note: One order in WP(C) 196 of 2001, which runs as a continuing mandamus with many orders across two decades. It governs ICDS and Anganwadi Centres; the mid-day-meal directions sit in separate orders of the same petition. Much of the wider relief was later absorbed into the National Food Security Act, 2013. Cite the specific order and date, never the case in the abstract.

judgments.case: Prakash Singh v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Issued seven binding directions on police reform, including fixed tenure, a State Security Commission, and separation of investigation from law and order.
judgments.what_changed: The reference point for every police-accountability argument in India, and a demonstration of how far court directions can go unimplemented.
judgments.status_note: Compliance across States has been partial and, by the Court's own later findings, frequently evaded through nominal legislation. Cite it for the standard, not for the state of affairs.
judgments.source_title: Prakash Singh & Ors vs Union Of India And Ors on 22 September, 2006

judgments.case: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (mid-day meal directions)
judgments.source_title: Interim Order of 2 May 2003, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 196 of 2001
judgments.holding: Restates and enforces the Court's direction of 28 November 2001 that every child in every government and government-assisted primary school receive a cooked mid-day meal of at least 300 calories and 8–12 grams of protein, for a minimum of 200 school days, and requires States still giving dry rations to move to cooked meals on a fixed timetable.
judgments.what_changed: This is the order that made the mid-day meal an entitlement rather than a scheme, and the reason a cooked meal — not dry rations handed to a parent — is the compliance standard. It is the single most consequential piece of Indian right-to-food litigation for anyone working on school nutrition.
judgments.status_note: One order in WP(C) 196 of 2001, which ran as a continuing mandamus for two decades. The mid-day meal is now statutory under the National Food Security Act, 2013 and delivered as PM POSHAN; cite the Act for present obligations and this order for the entitlement's origin and for the cooked-meal standard.

verified.against: text of the 2 May 2003 interim order, hosted by ESCR-Net (Indian Kanoon does not index this order; the Supreme Court's own interim orders in this petition are not published as discrete documents)

judgments.case: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
judgments.holding: An eleven-judge bench held that private unaided institutions have autonomy in administration and admissions, subject to regulation against maladministration.
judgments.what_changed: The governing authority on private education. It is what displaced the Unni Krishnan scheme, and it sets the limits of state regulation over private schools and colleges.
judgments.source_title: T.M.A.Pai Foundation & Ors vs State Of Karnataka & Ors on 31 October, 2002

judgments.case: Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra
judgments.holding: Sexual harassment does not require physical contact; conduct that outrages a woman's modesty and creates a hostile environment is enough to justify dismissal.
judgments.what_changed: Settled that an employer may act on non-contact conduct — advances, propositioning, sustained unwelcome attention — and that a disciplinary finding does not need the criminal standard of proof.
judgments.source_title: Apparel Export Promotion Council vs A.K. Chopra on 20 January, 1999

judgments.case: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh
judgments.holding: Transfer of land in Scheduled Areas to non-tribals, including government leases to private mining companies, is void under the Fifth Schedule regime.
judgments.what_changed: The core authority against alienation of Adivasi land for extractive projects in Scheduled Areas.
judgments.status_note: Its reach has been contested and applied unevenly across States, and later benches have distinguished it on facts. Check the position in the specific State before relying on it.
judgments.source_title: Samatha vs State Of Andhra Pradesh And Ors on 11 July, 1997

judgments.case: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
judgments.holding: Absent a law on workplace sexual harassment, the Court framed binding guidelines under Article 32 and declared them enforceable until Parliament legislated.
judgments.what_changed: Gave every workplace a duty to constitute a complaints committee sixteen years before the POSH Act existed. Employers could no longer treat harassment as a private dispute between staff.
judgments.status_note: The Vishaka guidelines operated as binding law until the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 replaced them. Cite the Act for obligations; cite Vishaka for the reasoning the Act rests on.
judgments.source_title: Vishaka & Ors vs State Of Rajasthan & Ors on 13 August, 1997

judgments.case: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
judgments.holding: Laid down mandatory safeguards for arrest and detention — memo of arrest, informing a relative, medical examination, and a record.
judgments.what_changed: The checklist used in every custodial-violence complaint, and the standard against which an arrest is judged procedurally invalid.
judgments.status_note: The safeguards were largely written into the Criminal Procedure Code (Sections 41A to 41D and 46) and carried into the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Cite the statute for the duty and D.K. Basu for its origin.
judgments.source_title: Shri D.K. Basu,Ashok K. Johri vs State Of West Bengal,State Of U.P on 18 December, 1996

judgments.case: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Gave 'forest' its dictionary meaning regardless of ownership or classification, and placed forest governance under continuing court supervision.
judgments.what_changed: Extended forest protection to land never recorded as forest, and created the long-running supervisory jurisdiction that still governs diversion of forest land.
judgments.status_note: Runs as a continuing mandamus with hundreds of orders since 1996. Cite the specific order, not the case in the abstract.
judgments.source_title: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulkpad vs Union Of India & Ors on 12 December, 1996

judgments.case: M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu
judgments.holding: Directed elimination of child labour in hazardous industries with employer contributions to a welfare fund and compulsory education for the withdrawn child.
judgments.what_changed: Set the template of employer liability plus schooling that later child-labour policy is built on.
judgments.source_title: M.C. Mehta vs State Of Tamil Nadu And Others on 10 December, 1996

judgments.case: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal
judgments.holding: Denial of emergency medical treatment by a government hospital violates Article 21; the State must provide adequate emergency facilities.
judgments.what_changed: Gives a patient refused emergency care a constitutional claim, and compensation, rather than only a grievance.
judgments.source_title: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoorsamity Of Ors vs State Of West Bengal & Anr on 6 May, 1996

judgments.case: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Adopted the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle as part of Indian environmental law.
judgments.what_changed: Reversed the burden: a project proponent must show an activity is safe, rather than an objector proving harm. Underpins most environmental regulation arguments since.
judgments.source_title: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum vs Union Of India & Ors on 28 August, 1996

judgments.case: Consumer Education & Research Centre v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Consumer Education & Research Centre ... vs Union Of India & Others on 27 January, 1995
judgments.holding: The right to health and to a safe working environment is part of Article 21; asbestos workers were entitled to medical monitoring and compensation.
judgments.what_changed: Established occupational health as a constitutional right rather than a welfare benefit, and put the duty of monitoring on the employer.

judgments.case: Chameli Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
judgments.holding: The right to shelter is part of the right to life, extending beyond a roof to civic amenities that make a dwelling liveable.
judgments.what_changed: Used to argue that resettlement sites without water, sanitation or access are not compliance with a rehabilitation obligation.
judgments.source_title: Chameli Singh vs State Of U.P on 15 December, 1995

judgments.case: Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
judgments.holding: Recognised a fundamental right to free education up to age 14, and framed a scheme regulating private professional institutions.
judgments.what_changed: The direct ancestor of Article 21A and the RTE Act, 2009 — the reason elementary education is an entitlement rather than a service.
judgments.status_note: The scheme regulating private institutions was overruled by T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002). The right to elementary education survived and was constitutionalised as Article 21A. Do not cite the scheme; do cite the right.
judgments.source_title: Unni Krishnan, J.P. And Ors. Etc. Etc vs State Of Andhra Pradesh And Ors. Etc. Etc on 4 February, 1993

judgments.case: Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka
judgments.holding: Charging capitation fees was unconstitutional; the right to education flows from the right to life.
judgments.what_changed: First recognised a constitutional right to education, opening the line that ends in Article 21A and the RTE Act.
judgments.status_note: Substantially reworked a year later in Unni Krishnan and again by T.M.A. Pai (2002) on private institutions. Cite it for the origin of the right, not for the current law on fees.
judgments.source_title: Miss Mohini Jain vs State Of Karnataka And Ors on 30 July, 1992

judgments.case: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar
judgments.holding: The right to life includes the right to enjoy pollution-free water and air.
judgments.what_changed: Made environmental quality a fundamental-rights claim, which is why environmental PILs are brought under Article 32 rather than only under statute.
judgments.source_title: Subhash Kumar vs State Of Bihar And Ors on 9 January, 1991

judgments.case: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak)
judgments.holding: Established absolute liability: an enterprise in a hazardous activity is liable for harm without exceptions, and the measure of damages scales with its capacity to pay.
judgments.what_changed: Went beyond the English rule in Rylands v. Fletcher by removing every defence. The basis of India's industrial-disaster liability, including later statutory public-liability insurance.
judgments.source_title: M.C. Mehta And Anr vs Union Of India & Ors on 20 December, 1986

judgments.case: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
judgments.holding: The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood; pavement dwellers could not be evicted without due process, though eviction itself was permitted.
judgments.what_changed: The foundation of every procedural-fairness argument in Indian eviction and resettlement work — notice, hearing, and the fact that losing a dwelling means losing a living.
judgments.source_title: Olga Tellis & Ors vs Bombay Municipal Corporation & Ors. Etc on 10 July, 1985

judgments.case: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
judgments.holding: Treated a letter as a writ petition, relaxed standing, and held that bonded labour is a violation of Article 21 requiring identification, release and rehabilitation.
judgments.what_changed: One of the cases that built public interest litigation itself, and the authority for demanding rehabilitation rather than mere release in bonded-labour work.
judgments.source_title: Bandhua Mukti Morcha vs Union Of India & Others on 16 December, 1983

judgments.case: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
judgments.holding: Article 21 means more than animal existence: it includes living with human dignity and the bare necessities of life.
judgments.what_changed: The doctrinal root of the socio-economic rights line — nutrition, shelter and health arguments all trace back to this reading of Article 21.
judgments.source_title: Francis Coralie Mullin vs The Administrator, Union Territory Of ... on 13 January, 1981

judgments.case: Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand
judgments.holding: A municipality cannot plead lack of funds to escape its statutory duty to provide sanitation and abate a public nuisance.
judgments.what_changed: The standing answer to 'no budget'. Used across sanitation, drainage and solid-waste litigation against local bodies.
judgments.source_title: Municipal Council, Ratlam vs Shri Vardhichand & Ors on 29 July, 1980

judgments.case: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
judgments.holding: Undertrials detained longer than the maximum sentence must be released; speedy trial and free legal aid are part of Article 21.
judgments.what_changed: The origin of legal-aid and undertrial-review work, and the authority behind statutory undertrial release provisions.
judgments.source_title: Hussainara Khatoon & Ors vs Home Secretary, State Of Bihar, Govt. Of ... on 12 February, 1979

judgments.case: Safai Karamchari Andolan v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Safai Karamchari Andolan And Ors vs Union Of India And Ors on 27 March, 2014
judgments.holding: Held that the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013 expressly acknowledges the Article 17 and Article 21 rights of persons engaged in cleaning sewers, tanks and human excreta, and directed States to identify and rehabilitate all manual scavengers. Directed that entering a sewer without safety gear be treated as a crime even in an emergency, with ₹10 lakh compensation to the family for each death.
judgments.what_changed: Turns manual scavenging from a welfare problem into a rights violation with a named remedy. The ₹10 lakh figure and the sewer-death direction are what an organisation cites when a municipality or contractor sends a worker into a sewer without equipment.

verified.against: full text of the judgment on Indian Kanoon, document 6155772

judgments.case: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (Asiad workers)
judgments.source_title: People'S Union For Democratic Rights vs Union Of India & Others on 18 September, 1982
judgments.holding: Held that Article 23's ban on begar and other forms of forced labour binds everyone, not only the State, and that paying less than the minimum wage is itself forced labour, because a person accepting such work does so under the compulsion of economic circumstance rather than by choice.
judgments.what_changed: Makes underpayment actionable as a constitutional wrong rather than only a labour-law breach, and makes the principal liable for a contractor's conduct. It is the foundation of construction-site and contract-labour claims in India.

verified.against: full text of the judgment on Indian Kanoon, document 496663

judgments.case: Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Narmada Bachao Andolan vs Union Of India And Others on 18 October, 2000
judgments.holding: Permitted construction of the Sardar Sarovar dam to continue in stages, holding that relief and rehabilitation of displaced people must proceed pari passu with each increase in dam height, so that clearance for the next stage depends on rehabilitation actually keeping pace.
judgments.what_changed: Establishes rehabilitation-before-submergence as the test for large infrastructure, and gives oustees a sequencing argument rather than only a compensation claim. It is also the case most cited on how far a court will review a development project's merits — the majority declined to.

verified.against: full text of the judgment on Indian Kanoon, document 1938608

judgments.case: M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (Great Indian Bustard, undergrounding direction)
judgments.source_title: M.K. Ranjitsinh vs Union Of India on 19 April, 2021
judgments.holding: Directed that overhead power lines in Great Indian Bustard habitat be laid underground where technically feasible, with bird diverters installed in the interim, holding that conservation of a species facing extinction is an inseparable part of the right to life.
judgments.what_changed: The clearest instance of a court ordering infrastructure to be re-engineered for a species. It became the standard citation for conservation as an Article 21 interest — and then the standard example of how such an order fares when it meets energy policy.
judgments.status_note: Substantially revisited by the Court in its judgment of 19 December 2025, which replaced the blanket undergrounding direction with a revised priority-area regime after an expert committee report. Cite the later judgment for what is now required.

verified.against: full text of the judgment on Indian Kanoon, document 165550376

judgments.case: M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (revised priority areas)
judgments.source_title: M.K. Ranjitsinh vs Union Of India on 19 December, 2025
judgments.holding: Reworked the 2021 directions after an expert committee report: revised the priority-area map, required future lines in non-priority areas to run through designated power-line corridors, ordered aerial bunched cabling for lower-voltage lines and time-bound undergrounding of a defined 250 km of critical lines, rather than a general undergrounding requirement.
judgments.what_changed: Replaces a blanket engineering mandate with a mapped, staged one. Read alongside the 2021 order it is the clearest worked example in the docket of a court revisiting its own direction once implementation evidence arrives — which is what the status field on every other entry is trying to warn about.

verified.against: full text of the judgment on Indian Kanoon, document 197139120

judgments.case: Laxmi Mandal v. Deen Dayal Harinagar Hospital
judgments.source_title: Laxmi Mandal vs Deen Dayal Harinagar Hospital & Ors. on 4 June, 2010
judgments.holding: Two women below the poverty line were denied maternal care and the benefits they were entitled to under the Janani Suraksha Yojana, the ICDS, the National Maternity Benefit Scheme, the Antyodaya Anna Yojana and the National Family Benefit Scheme. The Court held that this engaged the right to health — including a right to a minimum standard of treatment and care in public facilities, and the reproductive rights of the mother — and the right to food, and that the schemes are interrelated so a failure in one is not answered by another.
judgments.what_changed: Made denial of maternity entitlements justiciable as a rights violation rather than a service shortfall, and treated the scheme architecture as one enforceable whole. Programme staff can be asked to show that a woman was actually enrolled and paid under each scheme she qualified for, not that the district ran a scheme.

checks: the five schemes named in the judgment

judgments.case: Social Jurist v. Government of NCT of Delhi
judgments.source_title: Social Jurist, A Lawyers Group vs Government Of Nct Of Delhi And Ors. on 22 March, 2007
judgments.holding: Private hospitals allotted public land at concessional rates had accepted, as a condition of allotment, an obligation to treat poor patients free — a proportion of inpatient and outpatient care and free casualty treatment. The Court took up their non-compliance, recorded that the hospitals did not dispute being bound by those terms even while asking for them to be reduced, and set up a committee with land and health officials to establish and monitor compliance.
judgments.what_changed: Established that a public subsidy carries an enforceable obligation that survives the moment of allotment. The reasoning transfers directly to any organisation given land, premises or concessional infrastructure on a stated public purpose: the condition is a continuing liability, not a formality at signature.

checks: free treatment condition on allotted land
the committee constituted by the order

judgments.case: Naz Foundation v. Government of NCT of Delhi
judgments.source_title: Naz Foundation vs Government Of Nct Of Delhi And Others on 2 July, 2009
judgments.holding: Read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code so far as it criminalised consensual sexual acts between adults in private, holding the provision to that extent inconsistent with the constitutional guarantees of dignity, equality and privacy.
judgments.what_changed: For four years it made outreach, testing and counselling work with men who have sex with men lawful to run openly, which is what public health organisations had argued for. Its later history is the point for anyone relying on a High Court ruling: a favourable decision can be set aside and the ground it cleared can close again.
judgments.status_note: Set aside by the Supreme Court in Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013), which restored Section 377 in full. The Supreme Court in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) overruled Koushal and reached substantially the position Naz had taken, so the law today matches this judgment's outcome — but it does so on the authority of Navtej, not of this decision. See the Navtej entry in this docket.

judgments.case: Sarang Yadwadkar v. Commissioner, Pune Municipal Corporation
judgments.source_title: Sarang Yadwadkar Ors vs Commissioner Pune Municipal ... on 11 July, 2013
judgments.holding: A municipal road was being built in a river bed, inside the mapped flood line. The Tribunal directed that nothing be constructed in the river bed within that line, that any part of the road falling inside it be carried on elevated pillars alone, that dumped debris be removed and relocated beyond the outer flood line applying the one-in-twenty-five-years rule, and that plantation and flood protection be undertaken along both banks.
judgments.what_changed: Put a hard line around the floodplain that a municipal project could not cross by treating it as already built. For anyone siting infrastructure, housing or a project office near a river, the mapped flood line is a constraint that binds the authority granting permission and not only the builder.

judgments.case: Vardhaman Kaushik v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Vardhaman Kaushik vs Union Of India on 27 July, 2018
judgments.holding: An order in the Tribunal's long-running Delhi air quality proceedings, consolidating and reiterating the directions made across earlier orders in the same matter — among them the bar of 11 December 2015 on registering diesel vehicles more than ten years old in Delhi.
judgments.what_changed: Shows what continuing mandamus looks like in an environmental matter: the relief is a series of directions kept under supervision over years rather than a single judgment. Useful to programme staff as a model of how sustained regulatory pressure is actually applied, and as a caution about how much of it depends on the forum staying seized of the case.

checks: recital of the 11 December 2015 diesel registration direction

judgments.case: Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kalpana Kakasaheb Gorade
judgments.source_title: The Oriental Insurance Co Ltd vs Kalpana Kakasaheb Gorade on 18 January, 2023
judgments.holding: A farmer's widow claimed under the Gopinath Mundhe Farmers Accident Scheme through the Taluka Agriculture Officer. The insurer repudiated on the ground that the death was a heart attack rather than an accident. The District Consumer Forum at Aurangabad allowed the complaint and directed the insurer to pay Rs 2 lakh from the date the claim was submitted, with interest at 6 per cent. On the insurer's appeal the State Commission found no reason to interfere and dismissed it, with no order as to costs.
judgments.what_changed: A worked example of a state welfare scheme being enforced against the insurer administering it, in the forum an ordinary claimant can actually reach. The route matters as much as the outcome: the claim went in through the agriculture officer, was refused there, and was recovered in a district consumer forum rather than a court. For anyone advising scheme beneficiaries, a repudiation letter is the start of a process and not the end of one.

checks: the District Forum order it reviews
the scheme named in the order

judgments.case: Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki
judgments.source_title: Pune Municipalc Corp.& Anr vs Harakchand Misirimal Solanki & Ors on 24 January, 2014
judgments.holding: On section 24(2) of the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013: where an award was made five years or more before the 2013 Act commenced and compensation had not been paid, the acquisition lapsed. The Court read "compensation has not been paid" strictly — money kept in the treasury rather than deposited in court did not count as paid.
judgments.what_changed: For six years this was the authority on which thousands of old acquisitions were reopened and land returned. It is in this docket because it was later overruled: anyone relying on an order that rested on it needs to know the ground moved.
judgments.status_note: Overruled by the five-judge Constitution Bench in Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal (6 March 2020), which held that tender or deposit of compensation suffices and that lapse requires neither possession taken nor compensation paid for five years or more. See the Indore entry in this docket.

checks: section 24(2) of the 2013 Act in issue

judgments.case: Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal
judgments.source_title: Indore Development Authority vs Manoharlal And Ors. Etc. on 6 March, 2020
judgments.holding: A five-judge Constitution Bench reconsidered section 24(2) of the 2013 Act on a reference. It held that an acquisition lapses only where the authority has neither taken possession nor paid compensation for five years or more, that tender or deposit of compensation counts as payment, and that periods covered by an interim order are excluded from the five years.
judgments.what_changed: Reversed the direction of travel for displaced landowners. Under the earlier rule a great many old acquisitions had lapsed for non-payment; under this one far fewer do. Any resettlement or land-rights case argued before March 2020 should be re-read against it, and any advice given on the older rule reconsidered.

checks: express reconsideration of Pune Municipal Corporation
the paid/tender question framed for decision

judgments.case: State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal
judgments.source_title: State Of Uttaranchal vs Balwant Singh Chaufal & Ors on 18 January, 2010
judgments.holding: Traced the history of public interest litigation and issued directions to curb its misuse. Courts must satisfy themselves about the credentials of the petitioner and the correctness of the contents before entertaining a petition, and should discourage petitions brought for publicity or private gain in the guise of public interest.
judgments.what_changed: Set the standard an organisation is now measured against when it litigates in the public interest. Credentials, bona fides and the accuracy of the pleadings are examined at the threshold, so a petition filed carelessly can be dismissed before its merits are reached.

judgments.case: Thalappalam Service Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. State of Kerala
judgments.source_title: Thalappalam Ser.Coop.Bank Ltd.& Ors vs State Of Kerala & Ors on 7 October, 2013
judgments.holding: A body is a "public authority" under section 2(h) of the Right to Information Act only if it is owned, controlled or substantially financed by government. Control must be substantial rather than merely regulatory or supervisory, and whether a given body is substantially financed is a question of fact to be decided case by case.
judgments.what_changed: This is the test that decides whether an organisation must answer RTI applications at all. It turns on the funding ratio and the degree of government control, so the answer can change as an organisation's grant mix changes — it is not settled once at registration.

judgments.case: ACIT (Exemptions) v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority
judgments.source_title: Assistant Commissioner Of Income Tax ... vs Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority on 19 October, 2022
judgments.holding: On the proviso to section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act and when a body pursuing the advancement of any other object of general public utility loses charitable status by charging for what it does. The Court set out when receipts from an activity carried on for a fee are compatible with charitable purpose, and when they take the body outside it, by reference to the quantitative limit in the proviso.
judgments.what_changed: Directly affects any organisation registered on the general-public-utility limb that charges for training, consultancy, evaluation or publications. What matters is the pricing and the share of total receipts, not the worthiness of the purpose, so a fee-earning programme can put the registration at risk.

checks: the percentage limit in the proviso discussed

judgments.case: New Noble Educational Society v. Chief Commissioner of Income Tax
judgments.source_title: M/S New Noble Educational Society vs The Chief Commissioner Of Income Tax 1 on 19 October, 2022
judgments.holding: On approval under section 10(23C)(vi) of the Income-tax Act for institutions existing "solely" for education. The Court held that solely means what it says: every object must relate to education. A surplus arising in the course of educational activity is not by itself fatal, but an object directed at profit disqualifies.
judgments.what_changed: An education organisation seeking this approval has to be able to point at its memorandum and show nothing in it pulls away from education. Objects added over the years for flexibility — consultancy, publishing, unrelated welfare work — are now the thing that costs the exemption.

judgments.case: S.P. Gupta v. President of India
judgments.source_title: S.P. Gupta vs President Of India And Ors. on 30 December, 1981
judgments.holding: Relaxed the rule of locus standi. Where a legal wrong is done to a person or a class who cannot themselves reach the court, by reason of poverty, disability or a socially or economically disadvantaged position, any member of the public acting bona fide may move the court on their behalf.
judgments.what_changed: This is why an organisation can litigate for a community rather than only for itself. Nearly every case in this docket that was brought by a union, a trust or a campaign rests on it. The bona fide requirement is also the hook later benches used to tighten who may file.

judgments.case: Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union ... vs Union Of India And Others on 13 November, 1980
judgments.holding: An early statement of widened standing in public interest matters, decided shortly before S.P. Gupta, on why access to the court has to expand when the interest at stake is collective rather than individual.
judgments.what_changed: Useful mainly as the step before the doctrine settled. It shows the reasoning being worked out rather than applied, which is worth reading if you are arguing at the edge of who may bring a case.

judgments.case: BALCO Employees Union v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Balco Employees Union (Regd.) vs Union Of India & Ors on 10 December, 2001
judgments.holding: A challenge to disinvestment brought as public interest litigation. The Court held that questions of economic policy are for the government and the legislature, and that the wisdom of a policy is not made justiciable by filing the challenge as a public interest petition.
judgments.what_changed: Marks where advocacy litigation stops. A petition attacking a policy choice as unwise will not get far; one attacking how a policy was made, or a failure to follow the law in carrying it out, is a different case. Framing decides the outcome more than merits do.

judgments.case: Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of West Bengal
judgments.source_title: Ashok Kumar Pandey vs The State Of West Bengal on 18 November, 2003
judgments.holding: On the scrutiny of motive in public interest litigation. The Court warned against petitions filed for publicity, private gain or at another's behest, and said courts should satisfy themselves about who is really behind a petition before entertaining it.
judgments.what_changed: Together with Balwant Singh Chaufal, this is what a court applies at the threshold. Who funded the petition, who is instructing, and why now are all fair questions, and an organisation that cannot answer them cleanly risks dismissal before the merits.

judgments.case: Holicow Pictures Pvt. Ltd. v. Prem Chandra Mishra
judgments.source_title: Holicow Pictures Pvt.Ltd vs Prem Chandra Mishra & Ors on 6 December, 2007
judgments.holding: Continued the line disciplining public interest litigation, on distinguishing a genuine public grievance from a private dispute dressed as one, and on the court's duty to examine that before proceeding.
judgments.what_changed: Completes the trio a court is likely to cite when it doubts a petition. Read with Balco and Ashok Kumar Pandey, it sets what an organisation should be able to demonstrate about its own standing before filing.

judgments.case: Neeraja Chaudhary v. State of Madhya Pradesh
judgments.source_title: Neeraja Chaudhary vs State Of M.P. on 8 May, 1984
judgments.holding: Releasing bonded labourers without rehabilitating them defeats the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976. Identification, release and rehabilitation are all constitutional obligations; a release order alone leaves people to return to bondage.
judgments.what_changed: The principle that a rescue is not an outcome. Any programme built around identification and release has to carry rehabilitation with it, and this is the authority for saying the state owes that part too.

judgments.case: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Indian Council For Enviro-Legal Action ... vs Union Of India And Ors.Etc on 13 February, 1996
judgments.holding: On chemical industry pollution at Bichhri in Rajasthan. The Court applied absolute liability and the polluter-pays principle, and held that the polluter must bear the cost of restoring the damaged environment, not merely compensate individual victims.
judgments.what_changed: Turned polluter-pays from a principle into a remediation bill. It is the authority for asking who funds the clean-up, which is usually the question a community actually needs answered.

judgments.case: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha
judgments.source_title: Municipal Corporation Of Gr. Mumbai vs Ankita Sinha on 7 October, 2021
judgments.holding: The National Green Tribunal has suo motu power under the NGT Act 2010; it may take up an environmental matter on its own rather than only on an application.
judgments.what_changed: Widens where an environmental problem can be raised. A newspaper report or a letter can start a matter without anyone having to construct an applicant with standing, which matters where the affected community cannot easily file.

judgments.case: Budhadev Karmaskar v. State of West Bengal
judgments.source_title: Budhadev Karmaskar vs State Of West Bengal on 24 August, 2011
judgments.holding: Arising from the killing of a sex worker, the Court held that sex workers are entitled to dignity under Article 21 and to the equal protection of the law, and went on to keep the matter alive for directions on their rehabilitation and treatment by police and the state.
judgments.what_changed: Established that outreach and welfare work with sex workers rests on a right, not on tolerance. The Court has continued to issue directions in the matter since, so what is currently required is found in the later orders rather than in this judgment alone.

judgments.case: Nipun Saxena v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Nipun Saxena vs Union Of India Ministry Of Home Affairs on 11 December, 2018
judgments.holding: On protecting the identity of victims of sexual offences, including child victims. The Court held that the identity must not be disclosed and gave directions covering reporting, records and support mechanisms.
judgments.what_changed: Binds anyone who documents or publishes casework. A case study, a photograph, a grant report or a social media post that lets a survivor be identified is not a communications judgement call — it is against the law.

judgments.case: Attorney General for India v. Satish
judgments.source_title: Attorney General For India vs Satish on 18 November, 2021
judgments.holding: Set aside the High Court's holding that "sexual assault" under the POCSO Act requires skin-to-skin contact. The essence of the offence is sexual intent, not whether there was direct contact with skin.
judgments.what_changed: Restored the protective width of the provision after a reading that would have taken a large class of assaults outside it. Worth knowing for anyone running child protection training, because the discarded interpretation circulated widely before it was overturned.

judgments.case: Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish
judgments.source_title: Just Rights For Children Alliance vs S. Harish on 23 September, 2024
judgments.holding: Viewing, storing or possessing child sexual exploitative material is an offence under section 15 of the POCSO Act and section 67B of the Information Technology Act, on the footing of constructive possession, whether or not there was any intention to transmit it. The Court also recommended replacing the term child pornography with child sexual exploitative and abuse material.
judgments.what_changed: Closes the possession gap that had been read into the provision. For organisations handling case material or running digital safety work, it also settles the terminology now expected in reporting and training.

judgments.case: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
judgments.source_title: Jarnail Singh vs Lachhmi Narain Gupta . on 26 September, 2018
judgments.holding: Refined the requirements laid down in M. Nagaraj for reservation in promotion. A state need not collect quantifiable data on the backwardness of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, but must show inadequacy of representation; and the creamy layer principle applies to exclude the advanced among them.
judgments.what_changed: Sets what a state has to be able to show before it reserves in promotions, and therefore what a representation audit has to measure. Relevant to anyone advising on affirmative action in public employment.

judgments.case: Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Prathvi Raj Chauhan vs Union Of India on 10 February, 2020
judgments.holding: Upheld the 2018 amendment to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, which Parliament passed to undo an earlier dilution of the Act. Anticipatory bail remains generally unavailable, save where the complaint on its face makes out no offence.
judgments.what_changed: Restored the Act to the strength Parliament intended after a period in which the safeguards had been read down. It is the current position for anyone supporting complainants under the Act.

judgments.case: Sukanya Shantha v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Sukanya Shantha vs Union Of India on 3 October, 2024
judgments.holding: Struck down caste-based segregation and division of labour in prisons as contrary to Articles 14, 15, 17 and 21. The Court directed states to revise their prison manuals and to remove the caste column from prison registers.
judgments.what_changed: Concrete, dated compliance obligations on every state, in a setting where discrimination had been written into the rulebook rather than merely tolerated. A checkable example for prison reform and anti-caste work of a manual being ordered rewritten.

judgments.case: Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (accessibility standards)
judgments.source_title: Rajive Raturi vs Union Of India on 8 November, 2024
judgments.holding: Held Rule 15 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Rules 2017 ultra vires the 2016 Act, because it made accessibility guidelines recommendatory where the Act requires a mandatory floor, and directed the Union to frame mandatory accessibility standards under section 40.
judgments.what_changed: Turns accessibility from something to aspire to into a standard that can be enforced. It came after years of non-compliance with the earlier phase of the same case, and the Court has stayed with it since — check the current orders, not only this one.

judgments.case: Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (compliance orders)
judgments.source_title: Dr. Balram Singh vs Union Of India on 20 January, 2026
judgments.holding: A compliance order in Writ Petition (C) No. 324/2020, the manual scavenging matter disposed of on 20 October 2023 and monitored since. The order sets out the direction it is enforcing: compensation for sewer deaths raised to Rs 30 lakh, being the current equivalent of the Rs 10 lakh fixed in 1993. It records the Union's affidavit that of 775 districts, a survey in 465 found no manual scavengers, and that 643 districts had uploaded certificates as at 22 November 2025.
judgments.what_changed: This is what enforcement of a landmark direction actually looks like three years on: a compensation figure that has to be claimed case by case, a district survey still incomplete, and a court that has not let go. If you work on sanitation-worker safety, the live orders are where the obligations are, not the 2023 judgment alone.

checks: the 20 October 2023 judgment named and cited as 2023 SCC OnLine SC 1386

judgments.case: Supriyo v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty vs Union Of India on 17 October, 2023
judgments.holding: A Constitution Bench declined to read marriage equality into the Special Marriage Act, holding that whether to recognise such marriages is for Parliament. It recorded the Union's undertaking to constitute a committee on entitlements for same-sex couples.
judgments.what_changed: Marks the current limit of what a court will do here and points the work at the legislature and at administrative entitlements instead. For organisations doing queer rights work, the practical route runs through the committee and through specific benefits, not through marriage.

checks: the Special Marriage Act in issue

judgments.case: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Anuradha Bhasin vs Union Of India on 10 January, 2020
judgments.holding: Freedom of speech and the freedom to carry on a trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g). An indefinite suspension of internet services is impermissible; orders must be published, reasoned, necessary and proportionate, and subject to periodic review.
judgments.what_changed: Gives something to challenge. A shutdown that disrupts teaching, cash transfers, telemedicine or reporting now has to exist as a published, reasoned order, and one that cannot be produced is one that can be contested.

judgments.case: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
judgments.source_title: The State Of Punjab vs Davinder Singh on 1 August, 2024
judgments.holding: A seven-judge Bench held that states may sub-classify within the Scheduled Castes to give preference to the most disadvantaged among them, provided the classification rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus and on empirical data, and does not corner the whole quota for one sub-group. E.V. Chinnaiah, which had held the Scheduled Castes to be a homogeneous class incapable of sub-division, was overruled.
judgments.what_changed: Changes the architecture of Scheduled Caste reservation and opens targeted affirmative action within it. It also puts a data burden on any state that sub-classifies, which is where advocacy and evidence work now bite.

judgments.case: Ajay Maken v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: Ajay Maken & Ors. vs Union Of India & Ors. on 18 March, 2019
judgments.holding: On the demolition of a settlement without rehabilitation. The Court treated housing as part of Article 21, set out a protocol of meaningful engagement with residents and a survey before any eviction, and held that a rehabilitation policy has to be applied rather than announced.
judgments.what_changed: The most developed Indian statement of what a public authority must do before it clears a settlement. It is the document to hold up when a demolition is announced without a survey, and it is why a rehabilitation policy on paper is not a defence.

judgments.case: Anita Kushwaha v. Pushap Sudan
judgments.source_title: Anita Kushwaha vs Pushap Sudan on 19 July, 2016
judgments.holding: Access to justice is a fundamental right under Articles 14 and 21. It has four components: an adjudicatory mechanism must exist, it must be reasonably accessible in distance, the process must be speedy, and the litigant must be able to afford it.
judgments.what_changed: Gives legal aid and paralegal work a constitutional footing rather than a charitable one, and names affordability and distance as rights questions. Useful wherever the barrier is that the forum is four hours away and costs a week's wages to reach.

judgments.case: National Campaign Committee for Central Legislation on Construction Labour v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: National Campaign Committee For ... vs Union Of India on 19 March, 2018
judgments.holding: On the cess collected for the welfare of building and other construction workers. The Court addressed its collection, the registration of workers, and the large sums lying unspent, and directed that the money be used for the workers it was raised from.
judgments.what_changed: Points at a welfare fund that already exists and is largely unspent. For anyone working with construction workers, registration is the gate to it, and this is the authority for asking a state board what it has collected and what it has disbursed.

checks: the construction workers cess in issue

judgments.case: Vanashakti v. Union of India (Vanashakti I)
judgments.source_title: Vanashakti vs Union Of India on 16 May, 2025
judgments.holding: Struck down the 2017 Notification and the 2021 Office Memorandum, which between them allowed a project begun without prior environmental clearance to be regularised afterwards. The Court held that an ex post facto clearance is alien to environmental jurisprudence and restrained the Central Government from issuing any similar instrument in future.
judgments.what_changed: For six months this was the strongest statement in Indian law that a project cannot build first and be cleared later. It is in this docket because of what happened next: it was recalled, reheard, and largely undone. Anyone who relied on it between May and November 2025 was relying on a judgment that no longer exists.
judgments.status_note: Recalled. A review moved by the Confederation of Real Estate Developers of India was allowed on 18 November 2025 by 2:1, with Bhuyan J. dissenting, and this judgment was recalled and the matters restored for fresh hearing. On rehearing, the judgment of 29 July 2026 upheld the 2017 Notification and quashed the 2021 Office Memorandum prospectively. See the 2026 entry, which is the governing position.

checks: the 2017 Notification and 2021 Office Memorandum in issue
the ex post facto holding, recited verbatim in the 29 July 2026 judgment
the recall and its 2:1 majority, recited in that judgment

judgments.case: Vanashakti v. Union of India (on rehearing)
judgments.source_title: Vanashakti vs Union Of India on 29 July, 2026
judgments.holding: On rehearing after the recall, the Court split the two instruments. The 2017 Notification is valid: a narrowly tailored, time-bound scheme traceable to section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act. The 2021 Office Memorandum is quashed, prospectively, because it created a perpetual amnesty by administrative instruction, supplanting delegated legislation, and offered no intelligible differentia for which projects qualify. Clearances already granted under either instrument stand unless individually challenged; no fresh application under either will be entertained; and the Central Government is restrained from granting ex post facto clearance by administrative order, save through a valid notification under section 3.
judgments.what_changed: This is the operative law on regularising a project built without clearance, and it is more permissive than the position that held for the previous fourteen months. Two practical points: an existing clearance granted under either instrument is not void and has to be attacked individually, and the route for new ones is closed. The Court also held that the well-known observations in Common Cause and Alembic must be read in their statutory context rather than as a general bar.

checks: bench of Surya Kant CJI, Joymalya Bagchi J. and Vipul M. Pancholi J.

judgments.case: In Re: Directions in the Matter of Demolition of Structures
judgments.source_title: IN RE: DIRECTIONS IN THE MATTER OF DEMOLITION OF STRUCTURES — 2024 INSC 866, [2024] 11 S.C.R. 722
judgments.holding: Laid down binding, pan-India procedure before any demolition. No demolition without a prior show cause notice, returnable either in the time the local municipal law allows or within 15 days of service, whichever is later. Service must be intimated digitally to the Collector or District Magistrate, who must designate a nodal officer and an email address for the purpose. The Court also required a reasoned order, an opportunity to be heard, and video recording of the demolition. Demolition ordered by a court is outside these directions.
judgments.what_changed: Turns a demolition from an administrative act into one with a paper trail somebody can test. The 15-day floor, the reasoned order and the video record are the three things to ask for when a settlement is served notice, and their absence is now itself a ground.

judgments.case: Avinash Mehrotra v. Union of India
judgments.source_title: AVINASH MEHROTRA versus UNION OF INDIA & ORS. — 2009 INSC 489, [2009] 5 S.C.R. 913
judgments.holding: Arising from a school fire in which many children died, the Court held that the right to education carries a right to be taught in a safe building, and issued directions on fire safety and building standards for schools.
judgments.what_changed: Makes the physical safety of a school a rights question rather than a facilities question. Anyone running or funding school infrastructure can be asked to evidence compliance, and a safety audit is not a nicety.

judgments.case: Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay
judgments.source_title: CENTRAL BOARD OF SECONDARY EDUCATION & ANR. versus ADITYA BANDOPADHYAY & ORS. — 2011 INSC 557, [2011] 11 S.C.R. 1028
judgments.holding: An examinee is entitled under the Right to Information Act to inspect their own evaluated answer book. The Court rejected the argument that an examining body holds answer scripts in a fiduciary capacity that would exempt them from disclosure.
judgments.what_changed: A working example of the fiduciary exemption being read narrowly, which is the exemption most often raised against an organisation asked for its own records. Useful well beyond examinations.

judgments.case: State of Tamil Nadu v. K. Shyam Sunder
judgments.source_title: STATE OF TAMIL NADU & ORS. versus K. SHYAM SUNDER & ORS. — 2011 INSC 555, [2011] 11 S.C.R. 1094
judgments.holding: On a state's attempt to undo a common school syllabus. The Court treated a child's entitlement to education of an equal quality, irrespective of economic or social background, as part of Article 21A, and declined to let the reform be reversed.
judgments.what_changed: Gives quality, not just access, a constitutional foothold. It is the authority to reach for when the argument is that a scheme delivers schooling of a visibly different standard to poorer children.

judgments.case: Environment & Consumer Protection Foundation v. Delhi Administration
judgments.source_title: ENVIRONMENT & CONSUMER PROTECTION FOUNDATION versus DELHI ADMINISTRATION & ORS. — 2012 INSC 442, [2012] 8 S.C.R. 1060
judgments.holding: Directed every state and union territory to provide toilets — with particular attention to girls — and drinking water in schools, within a fixed time, under the infrastructure norms of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act.
judgments.what_changed: Converted an infrastructure norm into a dated obligation on named authorities. It is the standing authority behind school WASH work, and the reason a missing girls' toilet is a legal failure and not a budget line waiting its turn.

judgments.case: DAV College Trust and Management Society v. Director of Public Instructions
judgments.source_title: COLLEGE TRUST AND MANAGEMENT SOCIETY & ORS. versus DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC INSTRUCTIONS & ORS. — 2019 INSC 1042, [2019] 12 S.C.R. 549
judgments.holding: A non-governmental organisation substantially financed by government, directly or indirectly, is a public authority under the Right to Information Act. Substantial financing does not require that government money be the majority of the funding; a large or significant share is enough.
judgments.what_changed: Extends the Thalappalam test specifically to NGOs and sets the threshold below a majority. An organisation whose grant income is a significant share of its total may be answerable to RTI applications without ever having considered itself a public body.
